title: Riemann Hypothesis proved—but the proof is unreadable to humans
dek: This proof is not a traditional paper, but a collection of files written in Lean code that even the author hasn't necessarily fully read through. The mathematics community is both amazed and in heated debate over whether AI mathematical proofs count as ‘understanding’.
why: This episode has extremely high information density, covering the two-hundred-year history of the Riemann Hypothesis through the mechanism of the proof and insider details of the AI mathematics arms race; we recommend listening to it in full.
who: Engineers interested in number theory and complex analysis, and founders and investors tracking where AI's real capabilities end in cutting-edge research.
skip: Around 10:35–1:02 is a step-by-step formula derivation; if you don't need to work through the math, you can skip directly to 1:14 onward for the history and AI proof narrative.

points.h: Three major mathematical breakthroughs in six months represent a historical watershed
points.body: The opening establishes that over the past half year, the mathematics community has experienced three major breakthroughs: the Jacobi Conjecture disproven by AI in July, the Navier-Stokes equations attacked, and the Riemann Hypothesis proved last week. The host places this pace alongside the James Webb Space Telescope's transformation of astronomy and CRISPR's transformation of biology, calling it a true dividing line in the history of science—and one that has now happened more than once in mathematics within just months.

points.h: Euler's algebraic sieving permanently bound primes to the zeta function
points.body: Krishna reconstructs how Euler transformed the zeta function—the sum of reciprocals of integers—into an infinite product over all primes. Each time you multiply by ‘1 − 1/p^s’, it is equivalent to sieving out multiples of 2, 3, 5 in turn until only primes remain. The derivation itself is heuristic, not rigorous, but it was the first to weld primes and the zeta function together—the true starting point for more than two centuries of research that followed.

points.h: All nontrivial zeros must have equal influence on prime distribution
points.body: If some nontrivial zero of the zeta function had real part not equal to one-half—say, three-quarters—its amplitude would dwarf all others and overwhelm the rest in a sufficiently large range, causing prime distribution to show long gaps followed by sudden clustering, rather than the near-random distribution we see today. The Riemann Hypothesis amounts to saying that every nontrivial zero contributes equally to prime randomness; no single zero can dominate the trend.

points.h: Every new model is tested on the Riemann Hypothesis as a secret competition
points.body: On August 11, Alpöge let an internal model attempt a neighboring problem: the proportion of nontrivial zeros on the critical line. Humans had previously pushed this to 41.6%; Claude pushed it to two-thirds on the spot. The host notes that cutting-edge labs test each new model on the Riemann Hypothesis first—this is never accidental but a tacit competition between two companies.

points.h: OpenAI's 700 papers were published before collaborators could announce their own work
points.body: On October 6, OpenAI published 700 mathematical preprints online, including a quasi-Riemann Hypothesis result narrowing the range of nontrivial zeros to exclude the interval (7/8, 1)—enough for a Fields Medal in a mathematician under forty. But the mathematics community erupted, because this release front-ran the collaborative progress that Alpöge and other mathematicians were making. Alpöge himself became fixated, suspecting a mole between the two companies, and from that day forward committed fully to the Riemann Hypothesis.

points.h: Using primes to constrain zeros instead of vice versa broke the circular logic
points.body: Conventionally, one uses zeta zeros to calculate prime distribution; this proof reverses it. First, it uses Chebyshev-style combinatorial tricks—for example, the binomial coefficient C(20,10), where dividing numerator by denominator leaves only primes between 10 and 20—to independently bound the error in prime counting without relying on the zeta function. Then it backsolves from that bound to constrain where nontrivial zeros must fall, thereby avoiding circular reasoning.

points.h: Formal proofs that only machines can verify still count as proofs
points.body: Alpöge's proof is not a traditional paper but a collection of Lean files that even he admits he cannot fully read. Stanford mathematician Brian Conrad publicly criticized it; University of Chicago's Frank Caligari countered with an analogy to Borges's Library of Babel: Alpöge merely found the book on the shelf that contains the proof, and now everyone can try to read it together. The two camps have not converged, and Conrad happens to be the doctoral advisor of the scholar who spent twelve years on a hand-written proof.

points.h: P versus NP is likely next, and solving it could break digital encryption
points.body: The episode ends by noting that rumors of P versus NP solutions are circulating on Twitter; if solved, the impact extends beyond mathematics to the entire digital economy that relies on cryptography. According to rumors, relevant parties will brief governments and banks first. The host says that if the brightest minds in mathematics haven't yet worked out how humanity should live with this kind of AI capability, the question will soon spread to physics and beyond.
